artwork.title: Woman with a Mirror
artwork.imageCredit: C2RMF scan via Wikimedia Commons · Public Domain

lessons.title: Two mirrors, no name

n1.text: A young woman with golden hair holds a long strand of it. Her other hand rests on a small jar. Behind her, a bearded man in red holds up two mirrors.

voice.speaker: titian
voice.text: Look past her face for a moment. Count the hands, then count the mirrors.

q1.text: Why does he hold two mirrors?

choices.label: So she sees front and back

b1a.text: We are the ones left out.

correction.tempting: She is looking towards the small mirror.
correction.truth: The small mirror faces her, so we see only its plain back. The two mirrors let her see herself front and back.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's gallery text (2017); Crowe and Cavalcaselle (1881); look at the photo.

b1b.text: Yes. He holds a big round mirror and a small square one. Together they let her see herself from the front and from behind, like a hand mirror held up to a wall mirror.

correction.tempting: There are two people and two mirrors.
correction.truth: He holds both, and they work together so that she can see her own back.
correction.evidence: The Louvre's gallery text (2017); Crowe and Cavalcaselle (1881).

n2.text: He stands half in shadow. The Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna, which borrowed her in 2021, calls him an admiring suitor. And she? Everyone asks who she was.

b2a.text: An old title, not a fact.

correction.tempting: In King Charles I's collection the picture was called 'Titian and his mistress'.
correction.truth: Nobody knows who she was. The Louvre names no sitter.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Crowe and Cavalcaselle (1881), who also saw no likeness of Titian in the man.

correction.tempting: She is a golden-haired beauty with a mirror.
correction.truth: Nothing marks a goddess: just two people, two mirrors, a jar and a stone ledge. Her name is unknown.
correction.evidence: Look at the photo; the Louvre record names no sitter, and Crowe and Cavalcaselle (1881) doubted the old names.

b2c.text: Right. The Louvre names no sitter. She is one of Venice's ideal beauties: the Louvre calls her the model of the Venetian ideal of a woman, and Vienna's museum speaks of belle Veneziane.

n3.text: As a young painter in Venice, Titian worked close to Giorgione, whom the Louvre calls his master. The Louvre still sees Giorgione here, in the stone ledge in front and the mirror.

voice.speaker: titian
voice.text: I was born in 1488 or 1490. When I was young, Giorgione was working in Venice too.

choices.label: The date is painted on it

b3a.text: A favourite answer, not a fact.

correction.tempting: The Vienna museum and a Louvre gallery text both say about 1515.
correction.truth: Even the Louvre disagrees with itself: its record says 1525 to 1550. No date is painted on the canvas.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record and gallery text (2017); the Kunsthistorisches Museum (2021).

correction.tempting: A date on the canvas would settle the argument.
correction.truth: No signature or date is visible on it, and the Louvre record lists no inscription. So the experts argue from style.
correction.evidence: Look at the photo; the Louvre record. The Louvre's two dates and Vienna's show the argument.

b3c.text: Right. The Louvre's record says 1525 to 1550; the Louvre's own 2017 gallery text and the Vienna museum say about 1515. There is no date on the canvas.

n4.text: Its later travels are better known. It belonged to King Charles I of England, whose collection called it 'Titian and his mistress'.

q4.text: Who sold it to Louis XIV?

correction.tempting: The king owned it before it reached France.
correction.truth: After Charles I, it belonged to Everhard Jabach of Paris, who sold it to Louis XIV.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Crowe and Cavalcaselle (1881).

b4b.text: Yes. After Charles I of England, the picture belonged to Everhard Jabach, a collector in Paris, who sold it to Louis XIV.

correction.tempting: He painted it, so it was his to sell first.
correction.truth: Its recorded owners run from Charles I of England to Everhard Jabach, then Louis XIV.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Crowe and Cavalcaselle (1881).

n5.text: From the king's collection it came to the Louvre. Vienna borrowed it in 2021 for an exhibition on Titian's women.

voice.speaker: titian
voice.text: Before you go, find the brightest spot of light in the picture. It is not on her skin.

b5a.text: Only on loan, for a few months.

correction.tempting: The Kunsthistorisches Museum showed her in 2021.
correction.truth: She went back to Paris. Today she hangs in the Louvre, in the room of the Mona Lisa.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record (exhibition list and room); the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

b5b.text: Yes: Room 711, the Salle des États, on Floor 1 of the Denon wing. Look for the two mirrors in the same room as the Mona Lisa.

correction.tempting: King Charles I of England owned the picture.
correction.truth: From Charles I it passed to Jabach and then to Louis XIV, and on to the Louvre.
correction.evidence: The Louvre record; Crowe and Cavalcaselle (1881).

n6.text: Two mirrors, a jar, a bare shoulder and a man in the shadows. Her name is lost and her date is argued, but she hangs in the room of the Mona Lisa. Take a minute with her.

lessons.takeaway: A man holds two mirrors so a Venetian beauty can see her back; nobody knows who she was, and even her date is argued.
